article.title: Henry Giroux on Why Elections Alone Can’t Defeat Fascism
article.author: Dick Price, Sharon Kyle
article.content: The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive. Three days after the November 3 midterms, Donald Trump named Stephen Miller his White House chief of staff. Republicans had lost control of Congress. For his new chief of staff, Trump turned to a longtime aide who helped shape his administration’s hard-line immigration policies. When Dick Price and I spoke with Henry A. Giroux, LA Progressive’s associate editor and a scholar of critical pedagogy at McMaster University, we wanted to know what Democrats could do with the opening voters had given them. Giroux had just taken up Miller’s promotion in his LA Progressive essay, “Trump’s Revenge Presidency: Stephen Miller and the Machinery of State Terror.” “Elections don’t defeat fascism,” Giroux told us. He welcomed the Democratic gains and the chance to limit the damage the administration could do. He also saw Miller’s promotion as a sign that Trump would double down in the face of an electoral rebuke. If voters had repudiated the administration, what would it take to challenge the conditions that had made its politics possible? Who feels the harm first? Giroux sees Miller as an architect of a governing project that brings together white nationalism, concentrated economic power, and the use of cruelty as a political tool. He traced its American roots through slavery, the dispossession of Indigenous peoples, and Jim Crow. Those histories, he argued, help explain how a society learns to accept the use of state power against some groups as an ordinary part of public life. I asked Henry how people come to recognize a system whose harms they experience so differently. Schooling is one form of education. People also learn from what happens to them and to those they love. People closest to exploitation often understand its workings through years of dealing with it. Those whose circumstances insulate them may begin to recognize the danger only when it reaches them. By then, the people who have been living with it all along have already paid a steep price. Giroux pushed back against the pessimism in my question. He spoke about people who had approached him after public talks and thanked him for giving them language for what they were living through. They could use that language to connect what they had been left to handle alone with decisions about whose needs count and who has the power to make those decisions. “The juice is in the connections,” he said. He sees neighborhoods, workplaces, classrooms, and movements as places where people can make those connections together. In his view, education becomes democratic when it helps people identify who holds power and gives them ways to hold that power accountable. He also argued that a media environment dominated by billionaires can flood people with information and still leave them with little sense of how one event connects to the next. For independent media and organizers, he said, the work is to tell a story that makes those relationships visible and gives people a way to imagine a society organized around different priorities. Related: Trump’s Revenge Presidency: Stephen Miller and the Machinery of State Terror What an affordability campaign can leave out Dick asked whether the midterm results also reflected a moral revulsion. The price of eggs and gasoline mattered. He thought voters could also have been responding to the brutality they saw in immigration enforcement, the suffering in Gaza, and the contempt Trump and Miller brought to public life. How could that revulsion become a movement capable of changing the institutions that had enabled those policies? Giroux welcomed campaigns that spoke to the cost of groceries and health care. His concern was what an agenda organized around affordability might leave untouched. A family can get some relief at the checkout counter while still facing racial discrimination, insecure work, or a political system that gives wealthy donors more influence than the people who live with the consequences. Affordability asks whether people can pay their bills. A democratic politics has to ask who has the power to shape the terms on which people work, live, and raise their children. That is where my longtime argument with Dick about the two major parties came back into the conversation. I have watched both parties court deep-pocketed interests while inequality grows. The November results give Democrats a chance to show whose interests they will serve when they have the power to set an agenda. That means looking at their votes, their donors, and what they are prepared to do when the two come into conflict. Related: Two Moralities, Two Futures: Youth in Revolt Against Gangster Capitalism What to do with the opening When I asked what people could do now, Giroux started with the promises candidates made to voters. Take those promises seriously, he said, and hold elected officials to them. He called for public scrutiny of campaign money, including support from pro-Israel groups such as AIPAC, and for organizing that can continue between elections. He pointed to mass protest, labor organizing, and strikes as ways people can exercise power together. There is a place for immediate reforms in that work. Giroux said he would support measures that protect people from being harmed now. His longer-term aim is what he called socialist democracy, which would require rebuilding institutions and shifting power toward the people whose lives are shaped by their decisions. For me, that is a test of whether we are serious about building a multiracial democracy. The people who have lived longest with racial exclusion and economic exploitation bring knowledge that should shape what gets built. How much democratic power we gain from this election will depend in part on whether those communities can set the agenda and hold the people elected in November to it.
